sections.html:
Tempe owners have three ways out: an agent listing, a do-it-yourself sale, or an as-is cash offer. Whichever you choose, the finish line in Maricopa County looks alike. A contract gets signed, a title company opens escrow, the county records a deed and a sales affidavit goes in with it.

Your choice drives the calendar. Listing puts the house in front of the most people, though showings, repairs and the buyer's loan and inspection windows all fall to you. A cash sale tends to pay less but has fewer steps and lets you set the closing date. With more renters than owners in town, plenty of Tempe sellers are landlords, heirs or owners of vacant houses, and each of those comes with extra paperwork.

Round up the following before you phone buyers:

  • Payoff amounts from each lender or lienholder on the house
  • The Maricopa County Assessor parcel number, which the sales affidavit asks for
  • Permit records for any addition, patio cover or garage conversion
  • Current leases and rental registration details if tenants live there
  • Your 2026 property tax statement from the Maricopa County Treasurer

The city is home to 190,571 people, 3.5% more than at the April 2020 estimates base. Only 42.3% of homes are owner-occupied. Owner-occupied homes carry a median value of $455,400, rent runs $1,743 at the median, and household income has a median of $79,663 across 78,279 households.

Those are citywide midpoints. A 1960s ranch near Tempe Town Lake and a townhome south of US 60 can sit far from them, so price your own house from recent sales on its street.

Buyers ask about commutes first, so lead with these:

  • Interstate 10 touches the western edge, Loop 202 crosses the north, Loop 101 follows the eastern border and US 60 runs east to west through the middle
  • Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport sits about 2 miles northwest
  • Valley Metro Rail serves Downtown Tempe and ASU, and the city runs free Orbit shuttle routes near the campus

The Tempe Elementary and Tempe Union High School districts cover most of the city. Kyrene (K to 8), Scottsdale Unified and Mesa Public Schools handle a few pockets, so verify your address with the district before a listing names one.

In the desert heat, the cooling system is the item buyers care about most. A unit that struggles in July is a bargaining point, and an old evaporative cooler or a roof with sun-cracked coating invites a request for a repair credit. When the unit is close to retirement, a written replacement quote in hand before listing keeps the figure under your control.

After any storm, check roof and window condition and keep the repair paperwork with your disclosure records.

Close out the permits on any work you did before you list. The Building Safety Division is at 31 East 5th Street, Garden Level East, east of Mill Avenue between 5th and 6th Streets. You can reach the permit center at PermitCenter@tempe.gov or 480-350-4311.

Plan review for residential work applies to single-family homes, duplexes and townhomes. New construction, additions, renovations, remodels and accessory structures need plan approval before a permit is issued, and the same staff answer accessory dwelling unit questions.

Suspect that an earlier owner built a room, carport or casita? Ask the division what is recorded for your address. Learning that before a buyer's agent asks gives you time to finish or close a permit instead of negotiating around it.

Every rental in Tempe must be registered with the Maricopa County Assessor's Office, and rentals of fewer than 30 days also need a city license. Check both before you sell a rented or recently rented house.

The rental housing code sets standards an inspecting buyer may notice. Landlords must provide:

  • Heating under the tenant's control that can bring habitable rooms to at least 70 degrees
  • Cooling that holds rooms at 82 degrees or less with air conditioning, or 88 degrees or less with evaporative cooling
  • Hot water at a minimum of 110 degrees
  • Landscaping in yard areas visible to the public

Anyone renting a property for 29 days or less needs a Tempe Short-Term Rental License, one per unit. The annual fee is $250, or $187.50 if issued after July 1, and licenses expire each January 1. Skipping the license risks a penalty as high as $1,000 per month. Owners must show $500,000 or more in liability coverage, notify adjacent neighbors and carry a state transaction privilege tax license. Questions go to Tempe Tax and License at 480-350-2955 or license@tempe.gov, including whether a license stays with the property after a sale.

sections.h2: Property tax and payoff at closing
sections.html:
Property tax on a Tempe house is billed and collected by the county rather than the city. Statements come in two installments (A.R.S. 42-18052).

InstallmentDue dateDelinquent after 5 p.m.
First halfOctober 1November 1
Second halfMarch 1May 1

Bills above $100 paid in full escape interest through December 31. The escrow officer usually settles any balance from your proceeds, so have the title company request a payoff figure from the Treasurer. Not sure the first half of 2026 went through? A call to the Treasurer answers it.

Disagree with the assessed value? File a real property appeal with the County Assessor within 60 days of the Notice of Value. The appeal covers value and classification only, so a large bill alone is not grounds.

Deeds are recorded at the Maricopa County Recorder, 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200, Phoenix, which is open Monday to Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Recording usually costs $30 per document, with some exceptions, and you can file in person, by mail or electronically.

Each deed needs an Affidavit of Property Value, unless the transfer is exempt and the deed shows an exemption code. A.R.S. 11-1133 has the buyer and seller, or their agents, certify sale date, total price, financing type, parcel number and owner-occupied or rental use. An incomplete affidavit means the recorder must turn the deed away. Note that the sale date on the form is the day the contract was signed, rather than the closing date.

Your title company prepares and files this package, but read the affidavit before you sign it. A typical closing runs in order: the title company searches the record and requests payoffs, you and the buyer sign, funds are released, and the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Do I need a license to rent my Tempe house for a weekend or a week?
faqs.a: Yes. Tempe requires a Short-Term Rental License for rentals of 29 days or less, one license per unit, and you must apply before you list. The fee is $250 a year, or $187.50 if issued after July 1, and the license expires January 1.

faqs.q: Who do I pay property tax to on a Tempe house?
faqs.a: Payment goes to the Maricopa County Treasurer, and the City of Tempe does not collect it. The two installments fall due October 1 and March 1.

faqs.q: What form does Arizona require to record a deed in Tempe?
faqs.a: An Affidavit of Property Value, which is ADOR Form 82162, unless the transfer is exempt. A deed that qualifies for an exemption shows the statute and exemption code on its face. Without a complete affidavit or that code, the Maricopa County Recorder rejects it.

faqs.q: Where can I get permit records for my Tempe address?
faqs.a: Contact the Building Safety Division at PermitCenter@tempe.gov or 480-350-4311. Staff can tell you what permits are on file, which matters if a prior owner built an addition or accessory structure.

faqs.q: What if I have not paid the first half of my 2026 Tempe property tax?
faqs.a: Either pay it yourself or ask escrow to take it from the sale proceeds. Full-year taxes paid by December 31 avoid interest.
